summary:
The Red Frontier is a 3D educational simulation game designed for children aged 7 to 12, serving as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Players get a letter from NASA inviting them to live and work at an outpost on Mars, where they carry out missions consisting of tasks such as gathering samples, locating ice deposits, and repairing equipment. Story Mode takes players along a guided path with fixed resources and events, whereas Free Play randomizes everything, making each run unique. The events are drawn from real NASA data gathered on Mars, and the lessons players unlock mirror what scientists discovered while landing rovers on the Red Planet. Players can also gather and examine Martian rocks to understand how they formed and why they are significant.

The game tackles this challenge by converting real mission decisions into hands-on practice for young learners. This matters because the shortage of astronauts and aerospace engineers keeps growing, and it begins with a lack of early passion. The Red Frontier is designed to ignite that passion.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Red Frontier is a 3D educational simulation game designed for children between the ages of 7 and 12. The player gets a letter from NASA inviting them to live on a Martian outpost and conduct research. Gameplay is divided into missions, which are broad categories consisting of tasks like collecting samples, locating ice deposits, and repairing equipment. Players move using standard WASD controls, the same scheme most modern games rely on. The home screen provides two modes. Story Mode follows a guided narrative with fixed resources and required events. Free Play randomizes every event, so players have to survive with whatever cards they’re dealt. Players also pick Easy, Medium, or Hard, which lowers resources, boosts damage, and increases event risk. A How to Play tab outlines the rules, and in-game lessons teach what real scientists learned when landing rovers on Mars. Players can gather rocks on the Martian terrain and examine them back at base, learning each rock’s significance, how it formed, and when NASA first discovered it, along with fun facts about Mars and its exploration.

Benefits

The game teaches real space science through play instead of lectures. Kids learn about Martian geology, problem-solving during missions, and the history of Mars exploration while having fun. Free Play and the difficulty levels keep it endlessly enjoyable, and the customization options (suit color, visor, patches, and more) reward progress. Every completed mission unlocks new items.

Intended impact

By introducing children to space exploration at an early age, we aim to inspire the next generation of students, astronauts, and engineers. The Red Frontier addresses the growing shortage of astronauts and aerospace engineers, which stems from a lack of passion, by building enthusiasm in kids and showing them how their choices can affect a Mars mission.

Our long-term goal is for the game to become an economically viable educational product that schools in many districts use. We intend to pitch the game to investors at local tournaments, rely on their guidance to obtain grants for further development, and pilot it with students and teachers so we can refine it for adoption by schools.

Tools and technology

Every idea and design concept for The Red Frontier was developed by our team.

Unity was used to build the game prototype

Claude AI were used to assist with coding

Authentic NASA data gathered on Mars to make in-game events realistic

Canva for our presentation

The game is played on PC

Creativity

The game combines education and entertainment, so learning feels like part of the adventure. Authentic NASA data and lessons taken from real rover landings are built into a card-style survival system. Free Play ensures every run is different, and the rock research feature transforms sample collecting into a lesson in Mars science.

Factors our team took into account

Audience: We designed for ages 7-12 and selected familiar WASD controls so kids can begin playing immediately.

Learning with fun: We wanted education to feel like part of the game, so lessons unlock as players advance.

Realism: We relied on authentic NASA Mars data, so events and lessons are rooted in actual missions.

Enjoyability and challenge: Story Mode, Free Play, and three difficulty levels allow different players to find the right level.

Onboarding: The How to Play tab and in-game lessons help new players get started.

Relevance: We directed the project at the aerospace talent shortage by fostering early interest.
